records.content_title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
records.content: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country’s occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina’s measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole-genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions. “As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude. Ars Video Importations In their analysis, health officials identified the first importation in a resident who fell ill with the telltale rash on January 12 after returning from a trip to South Carolina, where they were exposed to a person sick with measles. Genome sequencing found that the virus closely matched sequences from South Carolina cases. One close contact of the Washington case fell ill and was isolated. No other cases were linked to this importation. In a second importation event, South Carolina residents visited public places while infectious. As a result, four residents with close contact with the South Carolina visitors fell ill. While infectious, the four residents visited schools, healthcare facilities, and a church. Nine of their contacts and one person exposed in a public location fell ill, leading to a total cluster of 14 cases that spanned January 15 to February 17. In the third importation event, two state residents returned from South Carolina and fell ill on January 15 to 16. No additional cases were linked to these residents. Similarly, a fourth importation event occurred when a resident returned from travel. The person adhered to isolation and quarantine recommendations, and no cases were linked to this one. In the fifth importation event, a Washington state resident returned from out-of-state travel where they had contact with ill contacts and fell ill themselves on January 19. While contagious, they visited a school and a healthcare facility. Six close contacts fell ill. In all, this cluster of seven cases spanned January 19 to January 29. The genome sequences from five of the cases were nearly identical to those seen in South Carolina. Officials credit basic public health work of quarantines, isolation, and contact tracing with keeping the virus from spreading farther than it did. Contradicting Kennedy While the study highlights how readily this virus can spread among states amid declining vaccination, it also contradicts a common talking point from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy, a prominent anti-vaccine advocate, has downplayed the current measles surge in the US and aggressively defended against suggestions that his decades of anti-vaccine misinformation and disinformation have contributed to the surge in cases and drop in vaccination. Instead, Kennedy claims that there is a “global outbreak” and the US is “doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak.” Both claims are false . Dozens of other countries have lower case rates than the US. While some countries, including neighboring Canada and Mexico, are also seeing large increases in cases, the soaring case tally in the US is not being driven by international imports, but by domestic spread in under-vaccinated communities. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , only 18 of the country’s 4,588 confirmed measles cases this year were reported among international visitors. Of all the cases, 4,404 (96 percent) are linked to a domestic outbreak. The US has had 43 new outbreaks this year. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes. 58 Comments

records.content: Bill Belichick, Jordon Hudson breakup report catches UNC staffers off guard Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping Holidays OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Measles Add Topic Measles cases in Ohio nearly 600% higher in 2026 compared to 2025 Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 30, 2026, 11:08 a.m. ET Hear this story Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with cases surging in Southern Ohio. Measles cases in Ohio and nationwide have reached a 35-year high, driven by declining vaccination rates. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among individuals who have not been vaccinated. Measles surged in Southern Ohio as Pike County reported 20 new cases over the past week during Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026. Meanwhile, Akron Children's Hospital recently announced a possible measles exposure on Oct. 20 at its main hospital building. The state had 36 new cases in the past week, a 350% increase from the eight new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 296 cases in 24 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Oct. 22. That number is 557% greater than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing in recent weeks: 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Last week, Van Wert County in western Ohio joined the list, with Medina and Pike counties reporting their first measles cases the week before. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Oct. 23 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 4,730 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 1 Ashtabula: 47 (three new cases) Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 54 Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 10 (one new case) Knox: 5 Medina: 27 (nine new cases) Meigs: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Pike: 22 (20 new cases) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 11 (one new case) Tuscarawas: 13 Van Wert: 3 (two new cases) Vinton: 1 Wayne: 45 Wood: 1 The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least five people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 30, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading in Ohio? Hancock County Public Health reported one measles case in Findlay with possible exposure to the public at NWO Urgent Care on September 29 from 2:30–5:30 p.m. and Blanchard Valley Hospital Emergency Department the same day from 3:30–6:30 p.m. Geauga Public Health reports that individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

records.content: Your Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Ask AI Search Medscape News Canada How Canada Can Prevent the Next Measles Outbreak Carolyn Crist October 29, 2026 The nationwide measles outbreak — which resulted in more than 6400 cases across 10 provinces and territories in 2 years — has officially ended, according to the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC). The agency made its announcement after more than 2 months had passed since the last associated case was reported. Infectious diseases experts in Canada are cautiously optimistic but recommend vigilance for future outbreaks. “It’s helpful and a step in the right direction that this outbreak is now declared finished, but this is not the finish line. This is the starting gate,” Isaac Bogoch, MD, professor of medicine at the University of Toronto and infectious diseases specialist at Toronto General Hospital, told Medscape News Canada. “Measles represents the canary in the coal mine. It shows the chinks in the armor of public health systems,” he said. “You have to think about other vaccine-preventable diseases — such as influenza, polio, and tuberculosis — and I’m not sure if we’ve really taken the necessary steps to prevent subsequent outbreaks.” Measles Outbreak Response Measles was first eliminated in Canada in 1998. During the nearly 30 year-period when measles was considered eliminated (1998-2024), the country reported an average of 91 cases annually, with 0-752 each year. Following sustained transmission of the same virus strain for more than 1 year, PHAC announced in November 2025 that the country’s measles elimination status had been lost. Isaac Bogoch, MD “We never should have been in a position where a high-income country with a sound healthcare and public health system should lose our measles elimination status, but here we are,” said Bogoch. “The drivers are similar here and worldwide — we’ve been chipping away at public health initiatives through a lack of funding and a lack of trust.” The multijurisdictional outbreak began in New Brunswick with a patient who was exposed to measles outside Canada. Additional cases with symptom onset after October 24, 2024, were considered part of the outbreak if the measles virus sequence matched that of the first case or if epidemiologic evidence (such as direct contact with an outbreak-related case) supported a connection. As of October 26, 1126 measles cases have been reported so far this year, according to Canada’s measles and rubella weekly monitoring report. Two new cases unrelated to the multijurisdictional outbreak were reported in Quebec during October 11-17. Seven measles cases are being monitored in British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. During the past 2 years, more than 90% of cases occurred among people who were unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. “In the big picture of what we can do as healthcare professionals, the fundamental root of the issue is vaccination. We originally achieved measles elimination by having almost everyone vaccinated across Canada,” Matthew Muller, MD, PhD, medical director of infection prevention and control and an infectious diseases physician at St. Michael’s Hospital and Unity Health Toronto, told Medscape News Canada. “If we can achieve herd immunity with 95% of people being vaccinated, there’s no need for anyone to get measles, including vulnerable people who can’t be vaccinated,” he said. “I want healthcare workers to remember that measles isn’t just a rash and a fever — it can be a severe disease that leads to severe complications, and I don’t want to go back to seeing those develop.” Two doses of a measles-containing vaccine can provide strong protection against infection. Canadians — including healthcare professionals — should check with their provider or local public health unit to verify their measles vaccination status, PHAC said. Matthew Muller, MD, PhD “With vaccination, if the percentage falls below herd immunity, it’s like a forest getting too dry, and then a spark can ignite a wildfire,” Muller said. “If we have big areas in Canada where people aren’t vaccinated, then one case can trigger the fire that leads to a widespread outbreak.” Muller also serves as chair in the Ontario Provincial Infectious Diseases Advisory Committee on Infection Prevention and Control and has helped with guideline and policy development around infection prevention in Ontario hospitals. He and his colleagues have talked about the importance of vaccination — and of having conversations with patients about their vaccination status. “It’s important to have open and frank conversations, not shying away or making assumptions about why someone may not be vaccinated,” he said. “Listen to understand their concerns and then help debunk myths and be a resource for them.” Future Outbreak Preparation Along with vaccination conversations, healthcare providers in hospitals and community settings can remain prepared by looking for measles symptoms and handling suspected cases appropriately. “While it’s great that this current outbreak is under control, there will continue to be introduction of measles into the population, especially with our closest geographic neighbor [the United States] having an ongoing outbreak in various states. We need to keep our index of suspicion high for measles when presented with compatible symptoms,” Susy Hota, MD, medical director for infection prevention and control and division head of infectious diseases at University Health Network in Toronto, told Medscape News Canada. Clinics and ambulatory settings, in particular, may feel more vulnerable and less prepared when handling unannounced cases that walk in the door, she noted. As part of an infection control policy, clinics can implement protocols that encourage patients and staff to know their vaccination status, provide time for staff to receive vaccinations, and design clinic intake to protect vulnerable groups from infection. Susy Hota, MD For instance, when confirming patient appointments, staff scripts should ask about broad respiratory symptoms, as well as measles-specific signs, such as a new rash. If new symptoms are disclosed at sign-in, staff can isolate suspected cases and put systems in place to care for pregnant patients, those with weakened immune systems, and vulnerable patients who may experience severe symptoms, such as infants or older adults. Updating these protocols now can help when an unexpected case occurs in the future, Hota said. “While reviewing a previous case, we found that measles hadn’t been recognized as part of the initial differential review, and the patient traveled from that clinic area to the lab for blood collection, which was adjacent to the preadmission area and led to massive exposure that was difficult to track,” she said. “When you plan ahead, include measles as a possible diagnosis, and follow protocols, you can isolate the patient, wear the appropriate protective gear, obtain bloodwork in a safe way, and mitigate the risks of spread.” Bogoch, Muller, and Hota reported having no relevant financial relationships. records.content: The outbreak that contributed to Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025 was concentrated in historically under-vaccinated communities with close social networks across Canada, the US, Mexico, and beyond, creating opportunities for cross-border transmission, concludes a study published by The BMJ today. The researchers say the findings highlight the ongoing risk of measles resurgence in countries that have previously successfully controlled the disease, and underscore the importance of culturally tailored community engagement to build trust and confidence in vaccination and prevent future outbreaks. Canada achieved measles-free status in 1998 after introducing a two-dose vaccine schedule and a national catch-up programme for school-aged children, but lost it in November 2025 after a measles outbreak that involved several provinces. In Ontario, the outbreak disproportionately affected historically under-vaccinated communities - groups with historically low vaccine coverage and close social networks across Canada, the US, and Mexico. To better understand the course of this outbreak and its impact, researchers analysed measles cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period (28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025). The outbreak consisted of 2,377 cases (2,064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks. Most cases (90%) occurred among members of historically under‐vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2,377 cases, around three quarters (73%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2,121 (89%) were unvaccinated and 97 (4%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 admissions to hospital, 13 admissions to an intensive care unit, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis (brain inflammation ), and one infant death. Laboratory tests identified a distinct measles virus strain that was subsequently detected elsewhere in Canada, and in the US, Mexico, and the Netherlands due to close social ties within and between under-vaccinated communities combined with the high transmissibility of measles. The researchers acknowledge that their analysis is subject to limitations inherent to public health surveillance data, and note that the number of cases and associated complications may be higher than what is reported in the study. In addition, the proportion of cases in under-vaccinated communities is likely to be conservative, reflecting challenges in data collection for a variety of reasons, including mistrust among some community members and concerns from public health staff about the risk of stigmatization of affected groups during the outbreak. However, they say this measles outbreak illustrates the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of substantial immunity gaps within domestically and globally interconnected communities. Limited spillover beyond these communities also highlights a high degree of vaccine acceptance in the population at large and the success of local partners in closing immunity gaps as part of the outbreak response, they add. "Strengthening of immunisation systems, improving vaccine coverage, and sustaining culturally appropriate engagement to continue to build trust in immunisation will be essential to prevent future vaccine preventable disease outbreaks and to support re-establishing measles elimination," they conclude. In a linked editorial, Jennifer Nuzzo at Brown University School of Public Health warns that Canada's loss of elimination status signals growing vulnerability to infectious disease threats, even in well-resourced high-income countries. She argues that elimination requires not just high vaccination coverage, but also sensitive disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, rapid outbreak investigations, timely reporting, effective public health responses, and public trust. Failing to stop measles within national borders also makes it harder for countries around the world to keep the disease at bay, she adds. She urges countries to recommit to measles elimination "not simply to restore a designation, but to stop a dangerous, preventable disease and strengthen the public health systems that protect their own populations and those of their neighbours from other serious infectious threats." Source: Journal reference: Wilson, S. E., et al . (2026). Impact of a large measles outbreak associated with transmission in the Americas and Canada’s loss of measles elimination status: Descriptive cohort study. BMJ. (Getty Images) 1Comment Share topics: Measles Georgia Macon County MMR Unvaccinated CDC DPH Outbreak MACON COUNTY, Ga. (WGXA) — The Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) has confirmed three new measles cases in Macon County among unvaccinated individuals who had close contact with a previous case, bringing the state's 2026 total to 25. According to the DPH, all three individuals were unvaccinated and had been in close contact with an October 12 measles case. The individual they were in contact with said they had contact with someone with measles from Pennsylvania -- where an outbreak has surpassed 1,100 cases. The DPH emphasized that vaccination is the best protection against measles. Adding that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine for children: the first at 12–15 months and the second at 4–6 years. Parents who have questions should reach out to their healthcare provider. In 2025, only 10 cases of measles were reported. In 2026, there have already been 25 confirmed cases of measles. Photograph: George Frey/Getty Images Families in the US are opting for earlier measles vaccinations amid outbreak Parents are opting for a second shot of MMR vaccine sooner, which aligns with guidance in Germany, the UK and France Measles cases are accelerating in the US, with twice as many confirmed cases as last year, and more parents are opting for earlier vaccination – especially with the second dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which can be given as soon as four weeks after the first. Giving the second shot soon after the first aligns with what some other countries, such as Germany, the United Kingdom and France, recommend – and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also says it’s an option. “More parents have heard about doing it ‘early’,” said Elias Kass, a naturopathic physician and vaccine advocate in Seattle, Washington. The CDC typically recommends giving the first MMR shot after age one and the second between the ages of four and six. But Kass began recommending the MMRV shot, which combines the second MMR and chickenpox (varicella) into one, at 15 months of age when measles cases began increasing a few years ago. Additional 178 cases of measles reported by US health authorities amid outbreak Read more More parents are taking that recommendation now, he said, adding that their thinking is pretty straightforward: “There’s no reason to wait, measles is here now.” Margot Taylor, a mother in Chicago, has three young children with three different vaccination histories for the MMR vaccine. “All three of them are fully vaccinated, but it’s had to be accelerated because of all of these increasing cases,” Taylor said. “We’ve gone backwards so much.” Her oldest, born in 2019, received her shots at ages one and four. Measles “wasn’t on my radar”, Taylor said. “I wasn’t even thinking about it.” But with her second child, born in 2023, Taylor was surprised when the pediatrician recommended the second shot at age two. Chicago was battling a measles outbreak, so they went ahead with it. Her third child, born in 2025, received the first shot after her first birthday – and then the second shot only three months later, in June. Taylor worried the shots might not work as well if they were so early. But evidence shows the vaccines still work well at earlier ages; the recommendation to give the MMR dose between four and six years is based more on logistical concerns, to ensure children have both shots before they enter kindergarten and to cut down on doctors’ visits because other shots are also typically given at those ages. And Taylor knows how vital the MMR vaccines are. When her third daughter was too young to get the first dose, she was exposed to measles at an airport during the west Texas outbreak. When the baby, only a month old, developed a fever afterward, they rushed to the hospital and stayed in a negative-pressure room until the test was negative for measles. “I am relieved, and I still cannot say enough how grateful I am” for the vaccines, Taylor said. But she still wonders at the need to make these decisions at all. “I never thought that I would have to be learning the vaccine schedules,” she said. Germany had similar recommendations to the US until 2001, when an outbreak brought a wave of illness and death that led the country to recommend the first shot at 11 to 14 months and the second shot at 18 to 23 months. In 2020, they moved the second dose to four weeks after the first. “There’s absolutely no indication so far that any kid that has been vaccinated twice in any rhythm would have a higher risk of measles than someone who’s been vaccinated according to the old rule,” said Catherina Becker, a scientist in Germany. Her son was two and a half years old when he got his second measles vaccine – and that was delayed only because he was recovering from a case of chickenpox. The CDC should “absolutely” consider a stronger recommendation to give the second shot earlier, Becker said. Some parents are also choosing to get their babies the first shot at the age of six months – which the CDC recommends in areas with outbreaks, before international travel, and after exposure to measles. Those infants should also receive a third dose. If a mother was vaccinated against measles before a pregnancy, that immunity is shared in utero, so the baby is protected for the first few months of life. That’s why a third dose is recommended if infants receive the first dose early – because it’s possible the baby still has some maternal antibodies and thus doesn’t establish a strong response to a vaccine at six months. The second MMR shot is different from other boosters. Most people mount a strong response to the first shot, which is why only one shot was recommended until 1989. But scientists discovered that some people don’t respond to the first shot and need a second – which is why the booster was recommended. That’s also why people born before 1989 may need to get a second shot now. “It’s a second chance to respond for the first time,” Kass said. Becker looks to past outbreaks to understand the effectiveness of the shots. In a 1998 outbreak in Alaska, only 17 people were sickened at a school where nearly all students – some 2,186 in total – had received measles shots. She compared it with a 2010 outbreak at a Waldorf school in Germany where nearly half of the 300 students were unvaccinated and 71 people were sickened. “It shows you what the measles vaccine does for you – it protects you from getting this thing,” she said. Germany had similar recommendations to the US until 2001, when an outbreak brought a wave of illness and death that led the country to recommend the first shot at 11 to 14 months and the second shot at 18 to 23 months. In 2020, they moved the second dose to four weeks after the first. “There’s absolutely no indication so far that any kid that has been vaccinated twice in any rhythm would have a higher risk of measles than someone who’s been vaccinated according to the old rule,” said Catherina Becker, a scientist in Germany. Her son was two and a half years old when he got his second measles vaccine – and that was delayed only because he was recovering from a case of chickenpox. The CDC should “absolutely” consider a stronger recommendation to give the second shot earlier, Becker said. Some parents are also choosing to get their babies the first shot at the age of six months – which the CDC recommends in areas with outbreaks, before international travel, and after exposure to measles. Those infants should also receive a third dose. If a mother was vaccinated against measles before a pregnancy, that immunity is shared in utero, so the baby is protected for the first few months of life. That’s why a third dose is recommended if infants receive the first dose early – because it’s possible the baby still has some maternal antibodies and thus doesn’t establish a strong response to a vaccine at six months. The second MMR shot is different from other boosters. Most people mount a strong response to the first shot, which is why only one shot was recommended until 1989. But scientists discovered that some people don’t respond to the first shot and need a second – which is why the booster was recommended. That’s also why people born before 1989 may need to get a second shot now. “It’s a second chance to respond for the first time,” Kass said. Becker looks to past outbreaks to understand the effectiveness of the shots. In a 1998 outbreak in Alaska, only 17 people were sickened at a school where nearly all students – some 2,186 in total – had received measles shots. She compared it with a 2010 outbreak at a Waldorf school in Germany where nearly half of the 300 students were unvaccinated and 71 people were sickened. “It shows you what the measles vaccine does for you – it protects you from getting this thing,” she said. (WLUC) - Three cases of measles were announced by Public Health, Delta & Menominee Counties on Oct. 21, and the agency immediately began working with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services to investigate the outbreak and notify individuals who may have been exposed. PHDM Medical Director Dr. Robert S. Van Howe commented on the cases. “Considering what’s happening across the country we have to be prepared to have other outbreaks so we may be seeing more in the future,” Van Howe said. “I would encourage people to find out their immunization status. If they can get a hard record of their vaccine record.” Van Howe says a single case of measles can spread and ultimately infect up to 18 people. He shares that there is not a single symptom, but a series of symptoms to be aware of. “What typically happens is you have someone who has a high fever, (about) 103-104. They have (a) cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis with pink eye and they’ll have that for about three or four days,” said Van Howe. “And then they break out in a rash that starts on the forehead and then spreads down to the rest of the body.” Schools are often considered high-risk environments for the spread of measles because large numbers of students and staff spend extended periods of time together in classrooms, cafeterias, hallways, and on school buses. The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after and infected person exits a room. Gladstone Schools Superintendent Dr. Jay Kulbertis says they stay in communication with the health department and currently take necessary precautions. “Really just like any casual contact communicable disease we know which of our students are high risk,” said Kulbertis. “We’re doing disinfecting like we normally would during the flu season. And we’re watchful on anything that might happen on the student’s side.” Van Howe says vaccination is a critical component to prevent infection of the virus. “If you have someone who is exposed to someone who has measles and they have not been vaccinated, or don’t have documentation that they are immune, then they can get vaccinated within 72 hours and they can return to school,” Van Howe said. The MMR vaccine is a combination vaccine administered in a two-dose series. Public health officials say it is 97% effective in prevention of measles. records.content: News Sports Lifestyle Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Measles cases in Ohio nearly 600% higher in 2026 compared to 2025 Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 30, 2026, 11:08 a.m. ET Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with cases surging in Southern Ohio. Measles cases in Ohio and nationwide have reached a 35-year high, driven by declining vaccination rates. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among individuals who have not been vaccinated. Measles surged in Southern Ohio as Pike County reported 20 new cases over the past week during Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026. Meanwhile, Akron Children's Hospital recently announced a possible measles exposure on Oct. 20 at its main hospital building. The state had 36 new cases in the past week, a 350% increase from the eight new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 296 cases in 24 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Oct. 22. That number is 557% greater than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing in recent weeks: 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Last week, Van Wert County in western Ohio joined the list, with Medina and Pike counties reporting their first measles cases the week before. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Oct. 23 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 4,730 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 1 Ashtabula: 47 (three new cases) Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 54 Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 10 (one new case) Knox: 5 Medina: 27 (nine new cases) Meigs: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Pike: 22 (20 new cases) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 11 (one new case) Tuscarawas: 13 Van Wert: 3 (two new cases) Vinton: 1 Wayne: 45 Wood: 1 The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least five people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 30, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading in Ohio? Hancock County Public Health reported one measles case in Findlay with possible exposure to the public at NWO Urgent Care on September 29 from 2:30–5:30 p.m. and Blanchard Valley Hospital Emergency Department the same day from 3:30–6:30 p.m. Geauga Public Health reports that individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. records.content: KENTUCKY — Kentucky health officials and doctors said measles continues to spread in the state, where 197 cases have been reported as the U.S. has seen more than 4,500 confirmed cases so far this year, according to CDC data. Doctors said that trend highlights a central challenge in slowing the spread. “The thing that concerns me the most is we’re having spreading of a disease that is totally preventable. And it’s preventable through vaccination,” said Dr. Mark Burns, an infectious disease physician with UofL Health. “The thing that concerns me the most is we’re having spreading of a disease that is totally preventable. And it’s preventable through vaccination,” said Dr. Mark Burns, an infectious disease physician with UofL Health. Burns said lower vaccination rates are helping sustain the outbreak. “The major thing, however, is the fact that for some unexplained reason, we have increased numbers of people not getting the measles, mumps, rubella, the MMR vaccine,” Burns said. “And it’s the lack of vaccination that is sort of perpetuating this.” State health leaders also point to misinformation about vaccines as a factor contributing to lower rates. “And people who are, I think, quite honestly, are being misled and potentially placed at risk by people in leadership positions spreading incorrect and false information that is simply not based in medical science,” said Dr. Steven Stack, secretary of the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services. As the outbreak continues, Stack said it is becoming harder to identify the source of new cases. “The longer this goes on, it gets harder to discern or determine who has credit to whom,” Stack said. “So now there are instances where we cannot find where did they pick up the disease, which means that someone who was vulnerable to the disease was around someone else with it and nobody is aware of who was sick at the time who got the new person sick.” Health leaders said anyone who suspects they have measles should call their hospital or emergency department before arriving. That allows medical staff to take precautions and help protect other patients from potential exposure. The MMR vaccine is given in two doses and is approximately 97% effective against measles after both doses. Health officials said vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to protect against the virus

Herman | Flickr New York Gov. Kathy Hochul issued an executive order on Oct. 5 declaring a state disaster emergency in response to the ever-growing number of measles cases in rural New York, as well as similarly rising numbers in bordering states. The executive order follows a recent surge in measles cases, with 108 recorded incidents of the virus throughout New York State as of Oct. 3, seven of which were recorded in New York City. Measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause serious health complications, primarily in children under the age of five. The measles virus presents itself with symptoms in the form of a rash, later accompanied by conjunctivitis, a runny nose, cough and a high fever around 104 degrees Fahrenheit. According to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, the measles virus has the potential to infect nine in 10 people who come in close contact with an infected person through the air when they cough or sneeze or if the individual is not properly vaccinated. Complications from the virus can range from ear infections and diarrhea to more extreme conditions such as pneumonia, encephalitis, immune amnesia and, in rare cases, death. Measles death targets those under five that are under-immunized against the virus. Currently, the most effective protection against the virus is the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. The vaccine is administered in two doses, the single dose is around 93% effective at preventing measles and the second dose bumps the effectiveness to around 97%. New York’s measles cases are highly concentrated among under-immunized rural communities in 18 counties. As of Oct. 20, Otsego County had 21 reported cases, followed by Seneca County with 30 reported cases and Steuben County with 19 cases. The three counties are considered to be some of the lowest-income relative to other counties in New York State. Additionally, they are at a geographic disadvantage due to their remoteness and distance from major hospitals. Therefore, they are left to rely solely on rural medicine, which later begs the question of vaccination accessibility. Despite both geographic and financial hurdles, public hesitancy is attributed to the primary cause of the current spread of the virus. Since 2025, there has been a heightened level of skepticism and fearmongering surrounding vaccinations due to political shifts, the amplification of health misinformation on social media utilizing buzzwords and the start of the “new right” media age. State Senator Gustavo Rivera corroborated this in a statement, saying, “The concerning rise in measles cases is due to a decrease in childhood vaccines driven by misinformation and is causing a public health emergency.” Hochul also said, “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.” The measles outbreak follows a similar trend occurring across the nation. As of Oct. 15, 4,410 confirmed measles cases had been reported throughout 47 state jurisdictions. Per the CDC, “Measles was declared eliminated from the United States in 2000. However, since early 2025, U.S. measles cases have been increasing, and we’ve had several large outbreaks of more than 50 cases.” The surge of measles cases in rural New York ultimately underscores an ever-growing public health crisis that is driven by dropping vaccination rates and the rise of misinformation. As state officials work to implement emergency measures to protect the public, the outcome will heavily depend on how efficiently they can work to restore the public’s trust in routine immunizations to prevent the resurgence of highly contagious diseases like measles. 1 Like This Story Leave a Comment More to Discover More in News CUNY celebrates renamed ‘149 St-Hostos’ subway station Mamdani launches website facilitating access to mental health services in NYC Mamdani and Council Speaker Menin to ban horse-drawn carriages Man shot by ICE officer in NYC Container ship sinks near the Strait of Hormuz as shipping attacks increase CUNY receives $1.5M STEM research grant renewal from the Sloan Foundation About the Contributor Juliett Searles, Arts & Culture Editor Juliett Searles is the Arts & Culture Editor for The Ticker. Matt Rourke/AP hide caption toggle caption i Matt Rourke/AP The U.S. is grappling with its worst resurgence of measles in decades, with cases particularly high in the state of Pennsylvania. New data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows there have been more than 4,580 measles cases reported in 2026 across the U.S. as of Oct. 22, which is more than double the number for the whole of 2025. The vaccination status of 96% of those who contracted measles in 2026 was "Unvaccinated or Unknown," according to data from the CDC. Living Better Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status A measles outbreak across Pennsylvania has grown as officials urge residents to get fully vaccinated against the disease. At least 1,338 cases of measles have been confirmed in 44 counties across the state so far this year, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health on Friday. There were 21 new measles cases as of Oct. 21. More than 250 people have been hospitalized and 5 people have died, the department also said. In Lancaster and Mifflin counties, two of the counties with the highest number of cases, local Amish communities, which have low vaccination rates, are being impacted the most. Of the five who have died, three lived in Lancaster County On Thursday, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen held a roundtable with Mifflin County healthcare providers to assess their needs in combatting the disease. "Our state metrics and data tell part of the story of the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, but listening to the people on the ground caring for people in affected communities like Mifflin County is essential to refining our public health response," Bogen said in a statement. One of the best ways to protect oneself from getting the measles is vaccination, according to health officials. Two doses of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine known as MMR, is nearly 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. One dose is about 93% effective. In Pennsylvania, the health department said healthcare providers have seen more residents interested in getting vaccinated for measles. Across the state, more than 39,000 measles vaccines were administered during the first three weeks of October – higher than an average of 25,000 vaccines administered across the state in one month, the health department said. Health How to define a measles death Earlier this month, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a disaster emergency after rising measles cases. There have been over 160 confirmed measles across the state, according to Oct. 20 data from the New York State Department of Health. Utah has also experienced a high number of measles cases. More than 700 people in Utah have been diagnosed with measles this year, according to Oct. 20 data from the Utah Department of Health and Human Services. There have not been any measles diagnoses in the state in 3 weeks, according to the department. In South Carolina, which was dealing with an outbreak earlier this year, there have been at least 997 measles cases in 2026, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health. The outbreak ended in April.
